'''Arthur Herbert Copeland''' (June 22, 1898 [[Rochester, New York]] – July 6, 1970) was an American mathematician. He graduated from [[Harvard University]] in 1926<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=7614}}</ref> and taught at [[Rice University]] and the [[University of Michigan]]. His main interest was in the foundations of [[probability theory|probability]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://um2017.org/faculty-history/faculty/arthur-herbert-copeland |title=Arthur Herbert Copeland Sr. {{!}} Faculty History Project – U. of Michigan |access-date=2013-01-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171202102740/http://um2017.org/faculty-history/faculty/arthur-herbert-copeland |archive-date=2017-12-02 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20130415014940/http://www.gf.org/fellows/2956-arthur-herbert-copeland|title=Arthur Herbert Copeland - John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation}}</ref>

He worked with [[Paul Erdős]] on the [[Copeland-Erdős constant]]. His son, Arthur Herbert Copeland, Jr. (1926-2019), was also a mathematician.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/brattleboro/name/arthur-copeland-obituary?id=6787455 |title=Arthur H. Copeland|website=[[Legacy.com]] }}</ref>

Copeland published a paper about [[pairwise voting]], which was very similar to the work of [[Ramon Llull]] and [[Marquis de Condorcet]]. The system he described became known as "[[Copeland's method]]".
